passage: Darshan wanted to run before college in the mornings, but in the first week he managed it only once. His shoes were in the tin trunk under the stairs, the socks somewhere else, and by the time he'd found both, the bus to Sinnar was due. So on Sunday he changed the setup. He put the shoes, socks tucked inside, right beside his charpai, and told himself the goal was only ten minutes: to the Hanuman temple at the end of the lane and back. "Ten minutes?" his friend Madhav scoffed. "That's not running." But on Monday Darshan's feet touched the shoes the moment he woke. He ran to the temple and back. Four weeks later he was still going, sometimes further, but never less than the temple.

qa.q: Where did Darshan put his shoes on Sunday?
qa.a: Right beside his charpai, with the socks tucked inside.

qa.q: Why was Darshan happy to set such a small goal despite Madhav's scoffing?
qa.a: Darshan wanted a start easy enough to happen every day; after a week of failed tries, ten minutes felt achievable rather than embarrassing.

qa.q: Which two choices helped the habit survive its first weeks?
qa.a: Keeping the shoes where his feet land on waking, and making the target tiny, to the temple and back, so there was nothing to hunt for and little to dread.

qa.q: How might Madhav's view change after four weeks?
qa.a: Madhav, who laughed at ten minutes, may be surprised that Darshan is still running and sometimes going further.

grounding: A student lowers friction by keeping shoes by the bed and setting a ten-minute target, and the running habit lasts.

passage: Anders had tried to start running three times since moving to Uppsala for university, and each time it died in the second week. Dark mornings, a cold floor, shoes lost somewhere in the hall cupboard. This time his flatmate Emil suggested something different. "Make it stupidly easy." So every night Anders laid out his running tights, jacket and shoes on the chair by his bed, and set the target at ten minutes on the lake path, nothing more. On the first morning he nearly skipped it, but everything was right there, so he pulled on the tights still half asleep. Ten minutes felt almost too short. He came back pink-cheeked and a little proud. Three weeks later the chair still held his kit every night, and Emil had started joining him.

qa.q: Where did Anders lay out his running kit each night?
qa.a: On the chair by his bed.

qa.q: How did Anders feel after the first ten-minute run, and why?
qa.a: He felt a little proud; after three failed starts, doing it at all, even briefly, showed him this attempt might be different.

qa.q: Which choice made the first morning work when Anders nearly skipped?
qa.a: Having everything laid out the night before, so he could pull on the tights half asleep without any search or decision.

qa.q: What would change for Anders if Emil stopped joining him later?
qa.a: The kit on the chair and the small target would still carry the habit, since the ease of starting, not company, is what got it going.

grounding: A student lays out running kit by the bed and sets a ten-minute goal, which helps the habit survive its early weeks.

passage: In the girls' hostel at Nandini's college, the sports track opened at six, but Nandini's alarm usually lost to her blanket. Her roommate Sunaina, who ran every day, suggested a trick. "Keep your shoes by your pillow. Literally. And promise yourself only ten minutes." So Nandini put her shoes at the head of the bed and her track pants on the chair. The first morning she grumbled but stepped straight into them. On the track she jogged slowly for ten minutes and walked back. "That's it?" Sunaina teased. "That's it," Nandini said. The next week she began adding a lap, but only when she felt like it. The deal stayed ten minutes. After a month, the track guard knew her name.

qa.q: What time did the sports track open?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: Why might Nandini have been happy to answer "That's it" to the teasing?
qa.a: She knew the small target was the point; keeping the promise to herself mattered more than impressing Sunaina, and it felt good to have gone at all.

qa.q: What choice kept the habit going once Nandini began adding laps?
qa.a: Keeping the deal at ten minutes and adding laps only when she felt like it, so a tired day never made starting feel too big.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see Nandini's progress over the month?
qa.a: Sunaina, a daily runner, may be pleased that the simple trick worked and enjoy seeing a roommate who used to lose to the blanket become a regular.

grounding: A student keeps shoes by the pillow and a ten-minute target, lowering friction so the running habit survives.

passage:
Dear Jyoti,
Remember how I said I'd start running in January and you bet me a samosa I'd quit by the 10th? The old me would have lost. Every morning I had to hunt for shoes, socks and a clean T-shirt, and by then my blanket had won the argument.
So here's what changed. Every night the shoes go right beside my bed, socks stuffed inside, T-shirt folded on top. And my goal is only ten minutes, once round the hostel block. Ten! Some days I feel silly, it's so small. But on the cold mornings those ten minutes are the only reason I get out at all, and most days I end up doing twenty.
It's week five. I owe you nothing. 😊
Love,
Ankita

grounding: A student lays out running shoes by the bed and sets a ten-minute target, and the new habit survives its first weeks.

passage: Harish, you asked how I kept running this time when I quit three times last year? Okay. I'm Parul, and I am not a morning person. Last year I'd plan a proper five-kilometre run, and by day four I'd wake up, think five kilometres, and roll over. This time I did two things. First, I sleep in my track pants, and my shoes wait beside the bed with the laces already loose, so I can step straight in. Second, the promise is just ten minutes: out to the bus stand and back. Most days that's all I do. Some days I keep going. It's been two months now, and the shoes have left a faint mark on the floor tile. That mark makes me weirdly proud.

qa.q: What is Parul's ten-minute route?
qa.a: Out to the bus stand and back.

qa.q: Why did Parul roll over by day four last year?
qa.a: Picturing a full five kilometres made getting up feel huge, so staying in bed seemed like the reasonable choice in that sleepy moment.

qa.q: What two choices helped Parul's habit survive this time?
qa.a: Sleeping in track pants with loose-laced shoes by the bed, and promising only ten minutes; the start became nearly effortless and too small to argue with.

qa.q: What might Harish take from Parul's story?
qa.a: Harish might see that a new habit needs an easy start more than a big one, and try shrinking a goal of Harish's own.

grounding: A student sleeps in track pants beside ready shoes and promises only ten minutes, so the running habit lasts.

passage: Nandini lives across the corridor from me in the postgraduate hostel. At the start of term, she announced she would run every morning. The first week, I didn't see her run once. Then, one evening, I noticed her running shoes placed neatly beside her bed, socks tucked inside, and a note on the wall: 10 minutes. That's all. Next morning, at six, I heard her door. Through the window I saw her jog slowly around the hostel lawn and come back, still yawning. Twelve minutes, maybe. She did it again the next day, and the next. By the third week the note still said ten, but she was often gone for half an hour. I asked her once why only ten. She laughed. "Because I can't argue with ten, Gautam."

Week one, a Sunday night. Jeevan wanted to start running before college. Kamal, his roommate, watched him put his running shoes right by the bed, socks inside, water bottle next to them. "Only ten minutes," Jeevan said. "That's it." On Monday he stepped straight from the bed into the shoes and jogged around the colony park, grumbling. Ten minutes, done.

Week two, a rainy Thursday. The alarm rang and Jeevan groaned. But the shoes were right there, and ten minutes seemed silly to skip. He ran under the tin roofs of the lane and came back soaked, laughing.

Week five, a Saturday. Kamal woke to find Jeevan already back, sweaty, stretching. "How long?" "Twenty-five. The ten keeps turning into more." Kamal glanced at his own shoes, buried under a pile of laundry.

passage: Ritu, you think running came easily to me? Arre, sit down. I was a thin girl then, in my second year at college in Guwahati. I tried to start running three times. Each time I set my alarm for five and planned five kilometres. Each time I lasted maybe four days. The fourth time, my roommate Sunanda said, "Why do you make it so heavy? Just put your shoes by your bed and go for ten minutes." I thought it was a joke. But I did it. Shoes by the bed, socks inside. Ten minutes around the hostel. Some days I came back after exactly ten and felt a bit silly. But I never skipped, because it was so small. By the second month I was running forty minutes without trying. That's how Binita became the one who wakes the whole family for a morning walk now.

qa.a: Binita's running shoes.

qa.q: How did young Binita feel on days she came back after exactly ten minutes?
qa.a: Binita felt a bit silly, but still didn't skip, because the tiny target made it easy to keep going.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned the failed attempts into a lasting habit?
qa.a: Following Sunanda's advice to put the shoes by the bed and aim for just ten minutes, instead of five kilometres, made starting easy enough to survive the early weeks.

qa.q: How might Sunanda have felt seeing Binita keep running for months?
qa.a: Sunanda might have felt amused and proud that a simple suggestion worked better than all the heavy plans.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how laying out running shoes by the bed and a ten-minute target helped her running habit survive its first weeks.

passage:
December in Chandigarh was freezing, and Divyansh, twenty, had quit running three times already. Every morning the alarm went, he lay under the quilt thinking about finding socks and shoes in the dark, and went back to sleep.
His hostel friend Amandeep suggested a different approach. “Put your shoes and socks by the bed tonight. Your jacket on the chair. And don't plan a big run. Ten minutes.”
“Ten minutes is nothing.”
“That's the point.”
That night, Divyansh laid out everything. At 6:30 the alarm rang. It was bitterly cold. But the socks were right there. He pulled them on, grumbling, then the shoes. He ran for ten minutes, breath steaming.
By the end of January, he was running twenty-five minutes, five days a week. The shoes still went by the bed every night.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh lay out his shoes and socks?
qa.a: He laid them out by the bed.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel about the ten-minute target at first?
qa.a: He felt doubtful, saying ten minutes was nothing.

qa.q: Why did laying out the shoes and aiming for ten minutes help?
qa.a: It removed friction on cold mornings and made starting tiny, so the new habit survived its first weeks.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel seeing Divyansh running five days a week?
qa.a: Amandeep probably feels pleased and proud that the simple advice worked.

grounding: The passage shows a student lowering friction by laying out running shoes and starting with ten minutes, helping the habit survive cold weeks.

passage:
Ritu had wanted to start running for a year. She'd bought shoes in March. They were still in the box in August.
Her flatmate Vandana, who ran every morning, asked what stopped her.
“I don't know. I think of running forty minutes, and I feel tired before I start.”
“Who said forty?”
“Isn't that what people do?”
Vandana laughed. “Start with ten. And take the shoes out of the box tonight.”
That night Ritu put the shoes and a T-shirt beside her bed in their Hyderabad flat. The next morning she saw them before she saw her phone. She pulled them on and went around the colony park twice. Ten minutes exactly.
She came home red-faced and oddly proud. For the next three weeks, the shoes lived by the bed, and she didn't miss a single weekday.

qa.q: How many times did Ritu go around the colony park?
qa.a: She went around the colony park twice, ten minutes exactly.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel after her first ten-minute run?
qa.a: She felt red-faced and oddly proud.

qa.q: What two changes helped Ritu start?

qa.q: How might Vandana feel seeing the shoes by Ritu's bed?
qa.a: Vandana would likely feel happy and encouraged that the flatmate finally started.

“Nandini, you're running now?”
“Trying, Ujjwal. Day twelve.”
“You? You said running was torture.”
“It is. That's why I cheat.”
“Cheat how?”
“Two things. One: every night I put my shoes right next to the bed, with socks inside them. So in the morning I step into them before my brain can argue.”
“And two?”
“Ten minutes. That's all I ask myself. If I want to stop at ten, I stop.”
“Do you stop?”
“Some days. Most days I do fifteen or twenty, because I'm already out.”
“Ten sounds too easy.”
“It's supposed to be easy. Last year I tried an hour a day and quit in a week.”
Ujjwal thought about it. “Can I join you? Tomorrow?”
“Shoes by the bed tonight,” Nandini said. “Socks inside.”

passage:
The first three times I tried to start running, I lasted four days each. I'm Arohi, second-year BSc, and my plan was always big: five kilometres, six a.m., every day. By day four I'd wake up, think about the whole five kilometres and roll over.
This time my roommate Simran gave me two rules. One: put the running shoes next to the bed, socks inside, so my feet land on them. Two: the target is ten minutes. Not five kilometres. Ten minutes, even if I walk half of it.
It felt almost too easy. Some mornings I did exactly ten minutes and came back. Some mornings I kept going for twenty because I was already out.
It has been five weeks now. The shoes are still by the bed, a bit muddy. I don't argue with myself any more. Feet down, shoes on, out.

qa.a: Arohi put them next to the bed, with socks inside.

qa.a: Arohi feels calmer and more confident, no longer arguing each morning, whereas the big old plan made Arohi want to roll over.

qa.q: Why did Simran's two rules help the habit survive?
qa.a: The shoes by the bed removed effort from starting, and a ten-minute target made each morning easy to begin, so the habit lasted past the first weeks.

qa.a: Simran would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that the simple rules worked where Arohi's big plans had failed.

Athletics club coach's log — Vishal
Kavitha joined the club in July wanting to run before classes. The first two weeks she missed most sessions. She told me, "I set the alarm, then I have to find my shoes, change, fill a bottle, and by then I've decided to sleep."
We made two changes. She now lays out her shoes, clothes and bottle beside her bed every night. And I set her target at ten minutes of easy jogging, not the full team session. If she wants more, fine, but ten counts as a win.
Weeks three to six: she has turned up for eighteen of twenty mornings. She looks more relaxed on the track and has started adding a lap on her own. Yesterday she said, "It's weird, I don't even think about it now."
Next step: after two more weeks, I will offer her the full session, if she wants it.

qa.q: How many of twenty mornings did Kavitha turn up in weeks three to six?
qa.a: She turned up for eighteen of twenty mornings.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel in the early mornings before the changes?
qa.a: She felt put off and tired, because finding shoes, changing and filling a bottle made starting feel like too much, so she decided to sleep.

qa.q: Why did laying out her things and a ten-minute target help?
qa.a: It removed the small obstacles between the alarm and the track and made the goal easy enough to start every day, so the habit could settle in.

qa.q: How might the other runners in the club see Kavitha's change?
qa.a: They might be encouraged to see a teammate who missed most early sessions now turning up nearly every morning and adding laps on her own.

Thursday night, hostel room
Day 12 of the yoga thing. I, Yusuf, am shocked it's still going.
Last year I bought a mat and a whole sixty-minute plan, and the mat lived rolled up behind the door. Getting it out felt like a chore before the chore.
This time Lalit, who shares the room, said, "Unroll it once and leave it there. And do ten minutes. That's it." So the mat stays open next to my bed, and I literally step onto it when I get up. Ten minutes. Some days I stretch longer, some days I stop at exactly ten.
Today I was late for class and still did it, because it's already there and it's only ten minutes. Lalit keeps tripping on it and complaining.
Twelve days is my record. I'm quietly proud.
